reply: We suggest starting with an in‑line NIR transmission probe (average cost) to monitor water in the petroleum stream, and run a parallel lab‑scale MIR‑ATR measurement for comparison. First experiments should define detection limits, temperature effects, and calibration robustness.

report.title: In‑line water monitoring for petroleum stream

answer.text: It depends on the optical appearance of the stream; a transmission‑type NIR probe is the simplest likely‑sufficient option, with MIR‑ATR as a higher‑cost comparison.

risks: If the stream is turbid or contains emulsified water droplets, transmission may be attenuated, reducing signal.
High temperature may affect fiber durability and probe materials; need temperature‑rated fiber.
Water content may be below the detection capability of a simple NIR model without extensive calibration.
The mid-IR fibre link over the required distance is not shown to be feasible in the supplied material.

steps: Measure the transmission of the chosen mid-IR fibre over the planned link length, or plan the analyzer close to the measurement point.
Collect representative petroleum samples with known water contents (lab‑determined).
Measure each sample with the NIR transmission probe and with a laboratory MIR‑ATR setup (as in).
Develop separate chemometric calibration models for NIR and MIR‑ATR.
Validate each model on held‑out samples covering the expected water range.
Compare prediction errors and robustness to temperature variations.
feasibility.decisionBasis: If the NIR model meets the agreed detection limit and accuracy on validation samples, it can be deployed in‑line; otherwise consider MIR‑ATR or a combined approach.

premiseChecks.detail: MIR (ATR) needs mid-IR fibres, and the enquiry implies an analyzer away from the line (length not given). Measure the transmission over the planned length before committing, or plan the analyzer close to the measurement point.
